items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: in some cases if there was the latest Miles Davis, you know, you didn’t have to.

ctx.x: And sometimes they must have given you different — like some liner notes there’s comments about each individual song, and some of it’s more of a general thing. Did you have to tailor your writing to what the record label wanted?

You know you never got — at least I didn’t — you never got specific instructions. Notes are almost always assigned by the producer except for some big labels like RCA and Columbia when there was somebody hired to — but the smaller labels weren’t that stratified. But they had a public relations office. Bob Altschuler at Columbia would assign liner notes. And at RCA they also had people. But usually it was the producer. And you would not get very specific instructions because after a while people figured that you’d…

changed completely when LPs became CDs. Because the CDs were much smaller format, but not only that but they were sealed and the notes were inside in the booklet. So in the LP era you knew that your notes were on the back of the album and that people would go to record stores and they would read the liner notes before they bought the record. I mean in some cases if there was the latest Miles Davis, you know, you didn’t have to. So you were in a sense, you knew that you had an obligation to make the product…
